nameStory: This beetle gets its 'rough-coated' name from the coarse, bumpy texture covering its body, which feels like fine sandpaper when gently touched. The 'longhorn' part comes from its impressively long antennae that can stretch longer than its entire body, resembling the horns of a Texas longhorn steer. These dramatic antennae are actually sensory powerhouses, helping the beetle navigate and find mates in the dark crevices where it lives.
description: The Rough-coated Longhorned Beetle is a medium-sized brown to blackish beetle that looks like it's wearing a textured coat. True to its name, it sports exceptionally long, thread-like antennae that curve gracefully backward over its body. These beetles typically measure about half an inch to three-quarters of an inch long, with a somewhat flattened, elongated body shape. Like all longhorn beetles, they're wood-boring insects that spend much of their lives associated with dead or dying trees.

idTips.label: Long Antennae
idTips.description: Antennae are distinctly longer than the beetle's body, thread-like and segmented, often held curved backward in a graceful arc

idTips.label: Rough Texture
idTips.description: Body surface feels noticeably bumpy or granular to the touch, like fine sandpaper, rather than smooth and shiny

idTips.label: Brown-Black Coloring
idTips.description: Overall dark brown to blackish color, sometimes with slight bronze or reddish tints, appearing matte rather than glossy

idTips.label: Elongated Body
idTips.description: Body shape is noticeably longer than it is wide, with a somewhat flattened appearance when viewed from above

idTips.label: Wood Association
idTips.description: Usually found on, in, or near dead wood, logs, or dying trees, often with a faint woody or musty smell in the area

habitat: Look for Rough-coated Longhorned Beetles in mixed and deciduous forests throughout New England, particularly around dead or dying hardwood trees like oak, maple, and birch. They're often found under loose bark, in rotting logs, or emerging from wood where they spent their larval stage boring tunnels. You might spot them on warm days crawling on sun-warmed dead wood or tree stumps in forest clearings and woodland edges.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging from their winter hideouts in late spring, becoming more active as temperatures warm. Look for them crawling on dead logs or under loose bark during sunny afternoons.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity season when adults are most visible, mating, and laying eggs. This is your best time to spot them crawling on dead wood or occasionally attracted to lights at night.
seasonality.fall: Activity begins to decline as adults prepare for winter, though some may still be seen on warm autumn days. New larvae are developing inside dead wood but won't be visible.
seasonality.winter: Adults hibernate under bark, in log crevices, or in leaf litter and are rarely seen. The next generation continues developing as larvae inside dead wood throughout the cold months.

funFact: The larvae of this beetle are master wood sculptors, creating elaborate tunnel networks inside dead trees that can weaken the wood so thoroughly that a seemingly solid log will crumble like a dry cookie when picked up, revealing an intricate maze of perfectly round holes and galleries.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other dark longhorn beetles, but the distinctly rough, sandpaper-like texture sets it apart from shinier relatives. Remember: if it feels bumpy and has super-long antennae, you've likely found your rough-coated friend rather than a smooth longhorn species.
contextualKnowledge: Despite their intimidating long antennae and association with wood damage, these beetles are actually beneficial decomposers that help break down dead wood in forest ecosystems. They don't attack healthy, living trees and pose no threat to homes or structures.
compareHints: Since this is the only Ecyrus species in New England, compare it to other dark longhorn beetles by focusing on texture - most longhorns have smooth, sometimes shiny bodies, while this species has its distinctive rough, granular surface. Other longhorns in the region tend to be either much larger with more dramatic markings, or smaller with smoother bodies and different color patterns.
